title: Stars trails over Armazones
caption: Star trails looking west from Cerro Armazones, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at the ELT site, Cerro Armazones, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: Lines of dots stream across the sky above the summit of Cerro Armazones, with an instrument on the right. This multiple-exposure photograph was taken facing west from the summit of the 3046-metre-high mountain chosen as the home of ESO's Extremely Large Telescope.

Earth's rotation makes the entire night sky seem to revolve around the southern celestial pole. When several exposures are combined, every star's movement between frames is recorded as a dotted trail. Each dot is one frame, and the gaps show the pauses between them.

The equipment on the right is the Differential Image Motion Monitor, or DIMM. It measures atmospheric seeing, which describes how much turbulence in the air blurs and jiggles the image of a star. For a telescope as large as the ELT, a site with calm, steady air is essential, and measurements like these are part of judging whether a summit is suitable.

understand.summary: This is a stack of night-time photographs taken in visible light with a camera on Cerro Armazones. The exposure settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points. The dotted trails only appear because several separate exposures were combined.

explore: Seeing is one reason astronomers put telescopes on high mountains and even in space, since the less turbulent air light has to cross, the sharper the image can be. The DIMM helps quantify that.
alt: Dotted star trails across a night sky above a mountaintop, with an instrument on the right.
